cards.title: Simulating monotone real circuits with MLP gates
cards.formal: Is there a universal polynomial p such that every partial Boolean function F on n Boolean inputs computed by a monotone real circuit with s gates can be represented by a single monotone linear-programming gate of size at most p(s+1)? The gate may be any of the source’s six types; equivalently, it may be a strong max gate ℓ(y)=max{(c+Cy)ᵀx : Ax≤b+By, x≥0}, with B,C entrywise nonnegative. Representation means a finite optimum with ℓ(y)>0 on the YES inputs of F and ℓ(y)≤0 on its NO inputs. The simulation is existential and nonuniform, and is required only on the promised Boolean inputs.
cards.why: Would clarify whether linear-programming representations contain the full power of small monotone real circuits or instead form an incomparable model. This is a structural issue in monotone computation, with connections to feasible interpolation and the size of optimization representations.
cards.status_note: Read the original question, real-circuit and LP definitions, the full ECCC report and the 2019 author manuscript’s question after Corollary 6.11. Crossref publication metadata distinguishes actual July/December 2019 dates from the manuscript’s placeholders. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of the single-gate simulation target; subsequent real-circuit interpolation papers do not by themselves provide this simulation. Searches were not exhaustive and proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: The source proves that monotone real circuits cannot polynomially simulate certain weak MLP gates and leaves the converse question open.
The expanded author manuscript retains the converse question and spells out the duality between allowed LP gate types.

sentences: A monotone real circuit uses arbitrary monotone functions of at most two real arguments as gates.
The question asks whether its behavior on Boolean promises always has a polynomial-size representation by one monotone linear-programming gate.
The LP counts rows and internal variables and need only separate Boolean outputs by the sign of its optimum.
The reverse simulation direction is already known to fail on some functions.
The expanded 2019 manuscript retains this nonuniform representation question; allowing all six LP types can be expressed by the strong-max type through duality.

cards.definitions:
A partial Boolean function consists of a promise domain D⊆{0,1}ⁿ and F:D→{0,1}. The relevant functions are monotone on their promise: if u,v∈D, u≤v coordinatewise and F(u)=1, then F(v)=1. A monotone real circuit is a finite acyclic circuit whose inputs are y₁,…,yₙ and real constants, and whose internal gates compute arbitrary total functions g:ℝʲ→ℝ for 0≤j≤2 that are nondecreasing in every argument. Fan-out is unrestricted. Its size s counts internal gates, including any constant gates. No continuity, rationality, finite-description length or effective evaluability of a gate function is required. The circuit computes F when its output equals F(y) at every y∈D; intermediate values may be any reals. Outside D its output is unrestricted. This is not a circuit restricted to addition, multiplication or Boolean AND/OR gates. Monotone partial promises are compatible with monotone total extensions; adding a monotone unary threshold to a real circuit gives a Boolean extension with constant gate overhead if needed.

For a strong max MLP gate, choose finite integers m,r≥1, A∈ℝ^{m×r}, b∈ℝ^m, c∈ℝ^r, B∈ℝ^{m×n}_{≥0} and C∈ℝ^{r×n}_{≥0}. The input is y∈ℝⁿ, while x∈ℝ^r is the internal optimization variable. The gate value is the maximum of (c+Cy)ᵀx subject to Ax≤b+By and x≥0. For each fixed y this is a linear program in x. A value is defined only if the program has a finite attained optimum; infeasibility or unbounded objective yields an undefined value. On each promised Boolean input the representing gate must have a defined real value. No condition is imposed at other inputs. The output threshold is exactly zero, with strict positivity for 1 and nonpositivity for 0; exact outputs 1 and 0, called sharp representation in the source, are not demanded. Coefficients are arbitrary fixed reals, independent of y. Size is m+r, the number of rows plus the number of internal-variable columns of A; coefficient bit length, input arity and the effort of solving the LP are not this size measure. The row dimension of C must be r so that Cy has the same dimension as c.

The six source gate types are strong max as displayed, strong min with objective min(c+Cy)ᵀx and constraints Ax≥b+By, x≥0; and the four weak types obtained by setting C=0 or B=0 in either form. Thus every weak gate is a special case of a strong gate. Linear-programming duality converts a strong min gate to a strong max gate of the same rows-plus-columns size: min{(c+Cy)ᵀx:Ax≥b+By,x≥0} equals max{(b+By)ᵀu:Aᵀu≤c+Cy,u≥0} wherever a finite optimum exists. This exchanges B and C while preserving their nonnegativity and the finite-optimum promise. Therefore allowing any of the six types is equivalent here to allowing the single strong-max form. It does not establish that a weak gate always suffices.

The polynomial p is fixed independently of n,s,F and all circuit gate functions. The representing LP coefficients may depend on the entire function or circuit. There is no requirement to compute them in polynomial time from a description of arbitrary real gates. The question compares representation sizes, not Turing running times or rational bit complexity. It asks for one LP gate for the whole Boolean computation. A network of many strong LP gates, or equality with the original circuit on every real input, is a different requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer proves a universal polynomial bound on the size of a single allowed MLP representation for every monotone-real-circuit computation on the stated Boolean promise. A negative answer establishes failure of every such polynomial bound, not merely failure of a chosen LP construction or one weak gate type. The known separation in the reverse simulation direction does not answer this question.

context_blocks.title: The reverse direction is already separated
context_blocks.text: The source gives partial Boolean functions with small max-left MLP representations but superpolynomial monotone real circuit complexity. It then explicitly asks whether the converse simulation holds. Being smaller on one family does not establish that the MLP model contains every small monotone real computation.

context_blocks.title: LP size is a structural measure
context_blocks.text: Each gate represents the optimum of a parameterized linear program. The cost counts constraints and internal variables while allowing arbitrary real coefficients. This representation measure differs from the binary size and runtime of an LP solver.

context_blocks.title: One gate versus a circuit
context_blocks.text: The paper collapses circuits of a single weak gate type to one weak gate. It does not claim the analogous collapse for general strong-gate circuits. The saved question concerns representation by one gate of an allowed type, so these two simulation targets must remain distinct.

context_blocks.title: The later manuscript retains the question
context_blocks.text: The 2019 author manuscript repeats the question immediately after Corollary 6.11. Its feasible interpolation results connect the models to Lovász–Schrijver and Cutting Planes proof systems, motivating the comparison without equating this gate simulation with a proof-system simulation theorem.

cards.context:
The source gives partial Boolean functions with small max-left MLP representations but superpolynomial monotone real circuit complexity. It then explicitly asks whether the converse simulation holds. Being smaller on one family does not establish that the MLP model contains every small monotone real computation.

Each gate represents the optimum of a parameterized linear program. The cost counts constraints and internal variables while allowing arbitrary real coefficients. This representation measure differs from the binary size and runtime of an LP solver.

The paper collapses circuits of a single weak gate type to one weak gate. It does not claim the analogous collapse for general strong-gate circuits. The saved question concerns representation by one gate of an allowed type, so these two simulation targets must remain distinct.

The 2019 author manuscript repeats the question immediately after Corollary 6.11. Its feasible interpolation results connect the models to Lovász–Schrijver and Cutting Planes proof systems, motivating the comparison without equating this gate simulation with a proof-system simulation theorem.
